This positions us, like many other non-high-income countries (e.g.,
India, where global publishers often run only support operations
[5]), primarily consumers of games made elsewhere .
The most popular mobile games in Brazil (and India!), e.g., Free
Fire , Roblox , Candy Crush Saga [1, 2] are not only from overseas,
but filled with Deceptive Patterns (DPs) [30]. DPs, formerly known
as Dark Patterns [6], are manipulative designs exploiting user bi-
ases for commercial gain at the user’s expense. In games, they are
intensified by the industry’s shift to "predatory monetization," ob-
scuring true costs [27]. They can cause several harms [7, 23, 24],
and potentially worsen Gaming Disorder (GD) [32, 37]. Yes, games
are also full of DPs in W estern, E ducated, I ndustrialized, R ich, and

D emocratic (WEIRD) contexts. Digital exploitation is not geograph-
ically exclusive. The central question is therefore not if harm occurs
elsewhere, but: Do the vast differences in non-WEIRD contexts alter
the nature and magnitude of that harm? While players in WEIRD
countries, where most of these games are developed, face risks, this
paper argues that the harm can be systemically amplified in major
Global South markets.

2 The Creator-Consumer Divide as a Lens for
Understanding Systemic Player Vulnerability

This paper proposes the creator-consumer divide as a theoretical
construct: a structural schism between creation and consumption
contexts, where vulnerabilities are systemic, pre-existing, and capi-
talized upon via deliberate targeting or indifferent automation. The
divide has two nuances.
First, games as entertainment can lower players’ critical guard
[36], making them more susceptible to manipulative designs dis-
guised as ’part of the game.’ This effect is amplified when a signifi-
cant portion of the population lacks fundamental cognitive defenses,
a vulnerability stemming from deep-seated societal issues in the
Global South. The contrast between the United States (US) and
Brazil illustrates this asymmetry. The US poverty rate is 11.1% [31],
while in Brazil it is over double at 27.4% [14], indicating a more
widespread precarity, which is linked to stress-impaired decision-
making [16]. A paradox of high digital penetration (86.2% [8]) co-
existing with low functional literacy amplifies the situation. While
the US grapples with a substantial illiteracy rate affecting 18% of
its adults, a challenge concentrated mainly in specific minority
and low-income groups [26], Brazil’s issue is more pervasive. 29%
of Brazilians are functionally illiterate (stagnant since 2018), with
another 36% possessing only elementary literacy skills [19, 20]. It
suggests that over half the population may struggle with the criti-
cal thinking skills [34] necessary to defend against manipulative
practices and discourses. This national-scale vulnerability is dis-
tinct from the challenges within specific US communities. Cultural

CHI PLAY Companion ’25, October 13–16, 2025, Pittsburgh, PA, USA Darin, T.

particularities, such as authority norms, can compound these vul-
nerabilities, creating additional exploitation vectors that are also
likely distinct from the creator’s context.
Second, the power imbalance operates structurally through reg-
ulatory arbitrage, exploiting political contexts that, often due to
economic pressures, lack strong and enforceable consumer pro-
tection. Less stringent consumer protection frameworks in many
Global South markets permit the deployment of systems and mon-
etization models that would face greater scrutiny or be prohibited
in other regions, such as the European Union (EU), where coopera-
tion networks work to enhance consumer protection when playing
video games. For instance, while EU principles demand transparent
pricing and respect for consumer vulnerabilities in online gam-
ing [35], their absence in Brazil, as well as in other countries in
the Global South, means that models can systematically obscure
true costs, deny consumers the withdrawal right, and intention-
ally target the most vulnerable players without facing similar legal
repercussions.
So, to what extent does our current game and DP knowledge
apply to non-WEIRD contexts, as research in this topic originates
predominantly from WEIRD contexts [18] (e.g., [11, 13, 15, 22, 29])?
This bias, mirrored in psychology (where WEIRD populations are
12% globally but dominate studies [17]) and broad HCI research
[21], limits findings’ external validity for the global majority and
overlooks socio-economic nuances. From a decolonial perspective
[3, 10], the WEIRD-centricity is not merely a methodological over-
sight; it is a systemic issue. Still, it reflects a more profound power
imbalance, where WEIRD perspectives, values, and designs, includ-
ing those that embed DPs and predatory monetization, are often
uncritically exported and imposed upon diverse global audiences.
Novel DP cases in widely used apps in Brazil [9, 28], most of which
were developed elsewhere, suggest that the context may enable
new forms of exploitation. Is it purposeful or coincidental? Does it
matter?
The creator-consumer divide can serve as a lens to examine
both the impact of manipulative and exploitative game designs
and monetization models on Global South markets, as well as the
potential for a design considered safe in a WEIRD context to become
harmful when deployed in a non-WEIRD one.

3 A Speculative Perspective: Helena and The
Gilded Cage of Ouroboros Seed

This paper uses a speculative design extrapolation [12] to propose
a critical future artifact and an imagined scenario that asks: What
if the creator-consumer divide ensnares individuals in a cycle
where virtual escape consumes real-world essentials and erodes
civic integrity?

Imagine Helena, an archetype of the systemic vulnerability pre-
viously described. Overwhelmed by the precarity of her life, she
turns to her smartphone not just for distraction, but for the sense
of control and achievement her reality denies her. She discovers
Ouroboros Seed. Unlike the simple games she’s used to, it is a
polished title from a huge WEIRD-country-based studio, its ads
promising a vibrant world of community and growth. She doesn’t
know that its state-of-the-art AI engine was prohibited in its home
country for the invasive data extraction used to fuel in-game loops,
nor that it was deployed in Brazil through regulatory arbitrage.
Initially, the game delivers. Its AI-optimized loops provide a
comforting sense of progress, fostering a deep engagement that
soon becomes dependency. The system then creates personalized
crises that make progress dependent on either intense Grinding
[38] or a $18 Pay-to-Skip offer. For Helena, $18 is not disposable
income; it represents the portion of her monthly income for cooking
gas. Her inability to pay is her only defense. But at an AI-calculated
moment of peak desperation, the game presents a different kind
of offer: the ’Community Solidarity Pledge.’ It is not a demand
for immediate cash, but a subtle prompt to pledge a portion of
her upcoming government benefit, the Bolsa Família. Framed as
a pro-social commitment, not a purchase, and designed to exploit
the human bias for immediate relief over a future cost, the offer
bypasses her financial barrier. She sacrifices a piece of her real-
world safety net for a fleeting sense of success in her gilded cage.
But the exploitation does not end with her finances. The rich
psychological profile the AI built on Helena, identifying her anxi-
eties and moments of low cognitive resistance, is sold to political
campaigns for targeted disinformation during a contentious local
election, leveraging the same vulnerabilities the game monetized.

Artifact from the future : The Adaptive Engagement & Resource
Pathway Report for Ouroboros Seed’s developers (Annex A). The
dashboard dehumanizes Helena, reducing her to a set of quantified
vulnerabilities, such as being 92% Prone to ’reactive choices’ in
a ’Scarcity Context.’ It logs triggers designed to weaponize psy-
chological states like ’Scarcity + Anxiety’ and details the harm as
a ’Projected Redistribution’ of resources from her specific urban
district. The corporate euphemism calls a monetization push the
’Harvest Equinox’ seasonal event, and classifies manipulative tactics
as ’Narrative Anchors.’ A final note confirms her profile matches
a ’Civic Tier 2 pattern’ and is flagged for a third-party messaging
test cycle, pending a performative internal ethics review.

Critical Questions: How must HCI’s definition of ’harm’ in
games evolve when designs prey not on universal biases, but on
widespread, structural vulnerabilities? What are our distinct ethical
duties when games are deployed not into isolated pockets of vul-
nerability, but into entire markets where these conditions are the
norm? And when this results in a massive, unidirectional extraction
of value from the Global South, regardless of intent, is it not our
responsibility to name it for what it is: a new form of cognitive
colonialism?
Ouroboro’s speculative dystopia is a provocation. It aims to
make palpable the extreme and deeply inequitable harms that can
arise when the creator-consumer divide in gaming is pushed to its
potential extreme.

4 Toward a Decolonial Game and Play Research

Rooted in my perspective as a researcher from Brazil, this paper
used a speculative scenario to argue that the impact of deceptive
design in games (and potentially other apps) is not uniform. The
proposed theoretical construct, called the creator-consumer divide,
illustrates how the most insidious harm occurs when sophisticated
design exploits pre-existing, systemic vulnerabilities, preying on
the educational deficits, economic precarity, and regulatory gaps

Games Made Elsewhere, Harms Felt Here CHI PLAY Companion ’25, October 13–16, 2025, Pittsburgh, PA, USA

that societies like mine, mainly in the Global South, have already
inflicted upon their citizens. Informed by decolonial thought, this vi-
sion challenges the HCI and games communities to reflect on when
play becomes another frontier for extraction. This compels us to ask
how we can move beyond studying non-WEIRD contexts as mere
sources of data and toward building genuine, equitable partnerships
with communities in the Global South. What are our responsibilities
in co-creating research agendas and design paradigms that build
resilience rather than deepen the precarity of the already vulner-
able? It is not trivial. But ultimately, is the CHI PLAY community
willing to try?

question: Como o template de Operationalizing pode informar as ferramentas de apoio ao desenvolvedor propostas em From Understanding to Intervention, e o que ainda precisaria ser testado?
answer: O template documenta [[problema, contexto, solução, necessidades, riscos e exemplos que falham ou correspondem aos critérios]]. A agenda propõe ferramentas integradas a engines para identificar decisões potencialmente problemáticas e sugerir alternativas éticas, respeitando contexto e objetivos do desenvolvimento. Como síntese, descrições estruturadas poderiam fornecer conteúdo argumentado para essas sugestões, em vez de avisos triviais ou regras descontextualizadas. Mas preencher um template não produz automaticamente uma ferramenta inteligente, útil ou adotada. A agenda exige testes empíricos e reconhece rejeição quando ferramentas parecem limitar criatividade ou objetivos financeiros. [[Integração e eficácia permanecem propostas a investigar]], não resultados demonstrados pela comparação.

work. These patterns were identified through the gameplay experiences of the

research team, which consisted of two students (one undergraduate and one post-

To develop a radiant pattern model, the research team identified compo-
nents that would make the pattern as operationable as possible. This would

ensure that, when other researchers replicate the model, no questions or doubts

would arise about how to apply it. Initially, the pattern followed [ 22 ] model of

motivational patterns. However, it had to be redesigned to align with the refined

definition of a Radiant Pattern grounded on self-determination theory.

The first step in structuring the template was to define the problem that

a radiant pattern aims to address—typically, situations in digital games that

affect players’ gameplay. Since deceptive patterns are often used as solutions in

such cases, identifying a radiant pattern that achieves the same goal without

causing harm can offer a more ethical alternative in a way that could possibly

mitigate any negative consequences. However, a pattern is not present in all

games; its context varies. Therefore, a detailed description of the scenarios

and styles in which it can be used is required. After presenting the problem

and defining the context, we discussed how the pattern can solve the problem

in that context through a proposed solution . As the refined definition of a

radiant pattern is no longer about satisfying basic psychological needs, but rather

about mitigating the frustration associated with these needs, it is necessary to

explain how the pattern can promote players’ well-being by avoiding a decline in

autonomy, relatedness, and competence. Therefore, it is essential to demonstrate

how each pattern impacts each basic psychological need individually, providing

specific information on how it promotes each need without having a negative

effect.

As we design this structure, we consider scenarios in which applying this pat-
tern irregularly could cause the opposite effect of its intended purpose. Therefore,

we have identified situations in which the developer must what for so that the

pattern does not actually harm players. For a more expanded and applicable

of how these patterns can either benefit or harm players, we present exam-
ples of implementation . These examples illustrate situations in which the

patterns may be negative—failing to meet the refined definition of RP —or pos-
itive, aligning with that refined definition. To finish the template, as the patterns

were initially identified through the research team’s previous gaming experience,

we present the community with a list of good examples where this pattern is

applied. To better demonstrate and clarify the pattern, this example can be

accompanied by an illustration of its practical application.

5.1 Radiant Pattern Structure

Following the validation. We propose a consistent structural template to sup-
port the operationalization of this refined R P definition and to guide the iden-
tification, development, and documentation of specific Radiant Patterns. This

template, detailed in Table 1 , outlines the essential components to be considered

120 L. S. Filho and T. Darin

and described when articulating an RP. By providing a standardized format,

we aim to facilitate clear communication, enable comparative analysis between

different patterns, and support the creation of a robust, shareable repository of

these beneficial design elements. Each identified Pattern as an RP should follow

the same structural template.

Table 1. Structural Template for Radiant Game Design Patterns (RPs)

Template Component Brief Description

Name Evocative title for the RP.

Problem Game design issue the RP addresses.

Context Recommended scenarios for RP application.

Proposed Solution Core mechanic/interaction of the RP.

Avoiding Decrease in SDT
Needs

How the RP supports Autonomy, Competence,

and Relatedness.

Watch For Potential pitfalls and misapplications.

Implementation Examples
(Failing/Matching)

Contrasting correct and incorrect uses.

Good Examples Illustrative games/features using the RP.

Name. The name of a Radiant Pattern may be a single word or a phrase that

describes its fundamental concept. To establish a direct association between the

pattern and a positive experience for the player, it is recommended that names

be selected that evoke autonomy and a sense of accomplishment. Examples of

suitable names include creation, free, and evolution.

Problem. As [ 2 ] noted, patterns function as solutions to recurring problem

situations. Given that the objective of Radiant Patterns is to promote player

well-being, the problems they seek to address pertain to game design issues that

have a detrimental effect on players’ well-being or that fail to satisfy their basic

psychological needs. Consequently, each Radiant Pattern should be accompanied

by a description of the game design issue that this pattern aims to address.

Context. Each pattern should be accompanied by a description of recommended

scenarios and game styles in which it can be applied. Given that patterns possess

distinct characteristics, it is essential to define their recommended use within

the game context to ensure the pattern’s effectiveness in achieving its intended

positive outcomes.

Proposed Solution. As a solution to a recurring problem, each description

should present how the RP can effectively address the identified problem. The

proposed solution outlines how game mechanics can be implemented to enable

the pursuit of development goals while ensuring foundational player well-being.

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 121

Avoiding Decrease in Autonomy, Relatedness and Competence. The

pattern then continues with a description of how it supports the player’s basic

psychological needs. The three fundamental needs—autonomy, competence, and

relatedness—are addressed individually, with a thorough exposition of how each

pattern positively impacts them. These descriptions elucidate the manner in

which the needs are supported independently, thereby ensuring that the fulfill-
ment of one need does not interfere with the fulfillment of others.

Watch For. If implemented improperly or outside of the intended context, the

efficacy of patterns may be compromised. Therefore, it is essential to include

a description of how to minimize predictable risks, avoid frustrating implemen-
tations, and highlight examples of poor applications of the pattern. Additional

warnings should also be provided to help designers recognize and prevent poten-
tial issues.

Example of Implementations: Failing and Matching the RP Criteria.

As an extension of the “watch for” section, it is important to present examples

of pattern implementations that align with the criteria defined for Radiant Pat-
terns. Likewise, it is necessary to provide examples where the implementation

does not meet these criteria. This enables a more in-depth discussion on imple-
mentation strategies and key considerations to help mitigate potential obstacles.

Good Examples. As the identified patterns are based on mechanics already

present in existing games, it is essential to present a comprehensive list of games

that effectively incorporate these patterns. A visual representation of the pat-
tern’s practical application within a game can enrich the definition and offer

game developers a better understanding of its practical implementation.

5.2 Radiant Pattern Example

present its documentation as a Radiant Pattern following the structure (Table 2 ).

on shared experiences.

Context. Digital games where players interact with game systems and poten-
tially each other. Applicable across various genres (sandbox, platformers, creative

suites).

Proposed Solution. Allows players to create, customize, and collaborate on or

share scenarios using readily accessible tools and resources, deliberately avoiding

From Understanding to Intervention 95

software artifacts with real-time support and intervention. Extending the learn-
ing possibilities of such projects, we propose a focused research effort on two

types of software artifacts. First, player-assisting tools , such as browser exten-
sions or in-game overlays. Their main goal would be to help transfer the pattern

recognition skills games into immediate, contextual guidance. Such tools might

highlight potential DPs as they appear, explain their manipulative mechanisms

(drawing on the typologies and user reactions), and perhaps even suggest alter-
native actions derived from a validated repository.

The advantage provided herein is the immediate empowerment of players

within their interaction, upholding their right to informed choice, and alleviating

the sense of being “deceived” [ 38 ]. That could potentially enable players to bypass

choices that could harm their autonomy. However, these tools are not supposed to

trick the user into ‘making a better choice.’ That would also hurt their autonomy.

Moreover, as Xiao and Denoo discussed, advanced players or game platforms

might devise methods to circumvent or compromise the efficacy of such tools

[ 40 ]. Instead, these mechanisms should aim to enhance player agency by fostering

real-time awareness, not to diminish it by dictating choices. The core intention is

to transform potentially deceptive or manipulative encounters into opportunities

for informed decision-making.

There are specific concerns to consider. These tools must avoid alert fatigue

from excessive notifications and monitor subtle DPs across gaming interfaces

without generating high false positives. Additionally, they need to minimize

being seen as intrusive to maintain a positive gaming experience.

The second type would be developer-supported tools for major game

engines, which might proactively integrate ethical considerations into the devel-
opment process. The goal here is to support developer objectives that align

with player well-being. Plugging in the research on the root of DPs in design

development and the issues designers encounter, such tools could help identify

potentially problematic design decisions at development time and help design-
ers brainstorm healthier alternatives. They could check against predefined DPs

definitions derived from the vast literature that describes them and suggest eth-
ically informed alternatives from the proposed repertoire of different proposals

of positive design patterns.

The primary benefit is proactive, encouraging inherently ethical practices

and support for designers working towards creating healthier experiences, par-
ticularly when they might not have clear guidance or face strict time limits

[ 23 ]. This approach may help developers better consider, negotiate, and make

informed design decisions on how to be more ethically engaged in their work-
flows. Of course, there are potential challenges to be considered. They include the

difficulty of developing intelligent and context-aware tools that make practical

proposals to players instead of just giving trivial notifications. Also, developers

risk working around or dismissing such tools if they are perceived as creativity

limitations, too limiting in design choices, or conflict with perceived financial

objectives.

96 T. Darin and N. Carneiro

Of course, these tools’ successful adoption and efficacy would be influenced by

the industry’s willingness to embrace ethical design standards and integrate such

support. However, this integration is a necessary embodiment of ethical princi-
ples rather than a strategy to enhance tool efficacy. It requires a broader shift

towards embedding these standards deeply within development cultures. Besides,

developing such software products demands an insightful grasp of player psychol-
ogy founded on research surrounding cognitive bias and DPs and the pragmatics

of game development. Rigorous empirical testing will also be essential to guar-
antee that such tools are effective and easy to use, balance the empowerment of

both end-users and developers’ sustainable goals, and foster a healthy interactive

experience.

It is important to note that while designing developer-support tools is cru-
cial for fostering ethical game design practices, it is equally essential to recognize

the structural constraints within the game industry that may limit their adop-
tion and impact. Many monetization-related decisions are typically made not

by designers or developers but by higher-level stakeholders such as sharehold-
ers, executives, and product or monetization teams. These decision-makers often

have limited or no background in game development and primarily rely on key

performance indicators (KPIs) like player retention, session length, active user

base, and revenue metrics to drive design directives. As a result, developers and

designers may have little autonomy to reject manipulative practices, even when

they are aware of the ethical concerns surrounding DPs. Given this context, we

advocate for further empirical research – such as large-scale surveys or interviews

with industry professionals, especially within the mobile and live-ops sectors –

to better understand developers’ awareness of DPs, their perceived agency in

decision-making processes, and the organizational pressures they face. This line

of inquiry could help clarify how deeply knowledge and decision power regarding

DPs are distributed across different roles in game companies, potentially guiding

more targeted and feasible counter-strategies in the future.

3.3 Advancing Methods and Measures for Assessing Dark Pattern

Prevalence and Player Experience, Including Well-Being

Current HCI research excels at identifying and categorizing DPs, although not

as much within games, and provides critical explorations of their ethical and

psychological impacts [ 16 ]. Significant steps have been made toward evaluation

tools, such as the System Darkness Scale [ 30 ] that assess a system’s perceived

“darkness,” and frameworks like the ADD framework [ 8 ] for critically considering

DPs in children’s applications. While these analytical insights and identification

methods are foundational, we advocate for expanding efforts to develop and val-
idate robust methods and measures that can more directly and quantifiably

assess the impact of specific game design elements on player autonomy,

perceived manipulation, and holistic psychological well-being.

The aim is not merely to identify whether well-being is affected but to under-
stand and quantify this relationship with greater nuance, particularly when

evaluating the efficacy of proposed countermeasures. It involves developing or

principles supporting foundational well-being, such as actively considering player

autonomy, competence, and relatedness.

Radiant design is more than the absence of harm; it is the presence of thought-
ful, ethically-grounded design choices to ensure player well-being is not signifi-
cantly undermined while pursuing engaging experiences. True radiance implies

a constructive, positive orientation that may go beyond simply counteracting

manipulative techniques. This nuanced understanding is crucial as we advocate

for their broader adoption and exploration. A pattern could be neutral, nei-
ther dark nor particularly radiant. Radiant Patterns aim higher, representing a

conscious, positive design orientation focused on fostering healthier player-game

interactions, rather than merely existing as a negation of harmful practices. This

broader, more constructive view allows Radiant Patterns to be a guiding prin-
ciple for innovative game design, not just a corrective measure.

6.3 The Challenge to Evaluate Players Well-Being

Evaluating the well-being that these patterns may promote in players presents

significant challenges. [ 41 ] demonstrate that radiant patterns, in contrast to

deceptive ones, can raise awareness of ethical principles in digital games. How-
ever, evaluating the well-being that these patterns cause in players can be chal-
lenging. [ 41 ] work shows that radiant patterns, as opposed to deceptive ones, can

raise awareness of ethical precepts in digital games. However, it has not yet been

possible to investigate the real effects these patterns can have on well-being since

they need to be inserted into the context of a game to directly affect gameplay.

For gameplay to be complete, other factors affecting the player’s experience must

be considered, such as visual, sound, and graphic elements. Therefore, there is

a need to develop evaluation metrics that focus on radiant patterns in isolation

from other gameplay elements.

There is still no methodology to directly evaluate the well-being that these

patterns can cause in users. However, it is possible to assess aspects of intrinsic

motivation, such as autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which belong to

self-determination theory. This can be done mainly through instruments such

as the PENS scale [ 39 ] and the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) [ 33 ]. As [ 8 ]

describes, positive intrinsic motivation and need satisfaction are fundamental to

Player Experience because they affect the gameplay moment and the broader

impact on player well-being. However, what results from the pattern itself or

the experience resulting from all the aspects present in gameplay? We invite

academia and the gaming industry to investigate methodologies that can deter-
mine whether motivation is genuinely positive due to its connection with the

game or the result of using radiant patterns.

6.4 A Radiant Pattern Repository

Radiant Patterns face the challenge of market acceptance, as deceptive pat-
terns are designed strategies that are already well established, widely used, and

profitable, despite being ethically inappropriate. They are employed, even when

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 127

developers recognize their potential harm [ 1 ], which illustrates a complex indus-
try conflict. A next step in the evolution of Radiant Patterns would be to explore

how they can generate a return for the game industry, addressing the advantages

of Deceptive Patterns and making them more attractive to game developers.

This progress can be collaborative as Radiant patterns can be identified based

on players’ and researchers’ experiences with game mechanics. Applying the tem-
plate structure proposed in this work makes it possible to systematize the cre-
ation and documentation of these patterns. Thus, the Human-Computer Inter-
action (HCI) community and game developers can collaborate to identify and

refine new Radiant Patterns. This collaboration could lead to the development of

an open repository of standards, strengthening the creation of a gaming industry

guided by ethical principles and committed to promoting player well-being.

6.5 Study Limitations

Although a refined definition and a detailed structure for operationalization is

presented, no evaluations with players have yet been conducted to validate the

direct effects of Radiant Patterns on well-being. The difficulty in isolating the

effects of design patterns from other gameplay elements such as graphics, sound,

and narrative also compromises the accuracy of such assessments. Generalizing

these results may also be affected, as players’ perceptions of the patterns can

vary depending on their gaming experience, personal profiles, prior exposure to

games, and awareness of the consequences of digital design patterns.

Another important limitation concerns the practical adoption of these pat-
terns by the game industry. Although they offer an ethical alternative to decep-
tive patterns, Radiant Patterns have not yet demonstrated concrete commercial

viability. The adoption of such patterns may not offer game designers an imme-
diate return in terms of their key objectives, including engagement metrics and

financial performance.

7 Conclusion

This paper presents a refined definition of radiant patterns and a documentation

structure that serve as a template to help game developers as well researches to

identify and empirically validate radiant patterns for his operationalization. This

structure is exemplified through the implementation of a example of a refined

defined Radiant Pattern.

As a refined pattern built upon the Self-Determination Theory, we rein-
force that the basic psychological needs of players—autonomy, competence, and

relatedness—are not compromised by detrimental design decisions, preserving

current levels of need satisfaction as well avoiding adverse effects directly associ-
ated with psychological harm. In this work, the authors extend an invitation to

the Human-Computer Interaction community to contemplate the development

of ethical alternatives to deceptive patterns by employing our systematic tool to

collaboratively identify those alternatives.

question: Como combinar a discussão de PENS/IMI em Operationalizing com a agenda de métodos para autonomia, justiça, transparência e manipulação percebida?
answer: Operationalizing aponta [[PENS e IMI]] como caminhos para aspectos de necessidades e motivação, mas destaca confundimento entre padrão e experiência total do jogo. Os textos oferecem [[direções metodológicas complementares]], sem fornecer um protocolo único já validado que isole causalmente o efeito de qualquer padrão.

perceived manipulation, and holistic psychological well-being.

The aim is not merely to identify whether well-being is affected but to under-
stand and quantify this relationship with greater nuance, particularly when

evaluating the efficacy of proposed countermeasures. It involves developing or

From Understanding to Intervention 97

adapting specific player experience instruments, such as validated questionnaires

or carefully designed behavioral metrics, that explicitly capture core tenets of

ethical interaction. These instruments should focus on perceived autonomy, fair-
ness, transparency, the sense of being respected (or manipulated), and critical

aspects of psychological well-being, drawing inspiration from well-established

theories like the Self-Determination Theory [ 33 , 34 ]. Such measures would allow

researchers to move beyond general assessments of “darkness” to indicate how

specific patterns or their alternatives influence these fundamental human needs,

a necessary point of departure to investigate how to counteract them.

Building upon existing frameworks, we call for creating standardized yet

adaptable methodologies for evaluating both the presence and, crucially, the

impact of DPs across diverse game genres and monetization models. It includes

refining our approaches to measure the actual effect of interventions designed

to mitigate DPs or enhance player awareness. For example, understanding why

some educational interventions show limited impact on knowledge about DPs

matters [ 39 ] requires more sensitive evaluation protocols to determine true effi-
cacy and identify areas for improvement.

Addressing these challenges involves not only identifying the absence

of DPs but also evaluating the effectiveness of ethical design choices

in creating a positive, engaging game experience driven by genuine enjoyment,

not coercion. We can enhance our use of gameplay data by developing teleme-
try and behavioral analytics to uncover patterns that indicate compromised

player autonomy or manipulative mechanics. Integrating this data with qual-
itative insights and refined player experience tools can lead to a more compre-
hensive assessment. Additionally, we could improve methodologies for assessing

the prevalence of DPs in new games by combining expert evaluations tailored to

specific game types and monetization strategies, along with emerging automated

detection approaches where ethically appropriate.

Developing and adapting methods and validated measures is not an end in

itself. Instead, it is a step toward generating highly specific, empirically grounded

guidelines that practitioners can trust and readily apply. These methods will

allow us to move from general advice to concrete, evidence-backed recommen-
dations (e.g., “ To uphold player autonomy in reward systems, design X which
demonstrably leads to Y outcome in perceived fairness, as measured by Z ”). By

focusing on quantifiable impacts on core aspects of ethical player experience,

we can make assessments more systematic, comparable across studies, and ulti-
mately more impactful in driving real change in game design practices.

4 Forging Ahead: A Research Agenda

This position paper argued for systematically expanding the focus of HCI games

research regarding game DPs. It means moving from identifying what is problem-
atic to demonstrating what is possible. We urge a dedicated focus on interven-
tionist and practical methodologies that enrich and are enriched by our existing

foundational understanding of DPs, creating a robust cycle of theory and applica-
tion. The aim is not to offer definitive, one-size-fits-all solutions, as the landscape

question: Como a passagem de World Creation a Creative Suite e a adoção de níveis e variantes em Beyond Dark Patterns respondem a limites de contexto do template de Operationalizing?
answer: Operationalizing já exige [[contexto recomendado, solução e análise individual das necessidades]], mas exemplifica World Creation de maneira ampla. No estudo posterior, participantes observam que criação de cenários e customização de algo existente têm particularidades; World Creation passa a Creative Suite, abrangendo diferentes experiências criativas. O framework incorpora níveis progressivos e variantes ambientais para adaptar a implementação sem perder lógica central. A síntese identifica um refinamento de precisão e escopo, não a refutação do compromisso ético anterior. Problem. As [ 2 ] noted, patterns function as solutions to recurring problem

situations. Given that the objective of Radiant Patterns is to promote player

well-being, the problems they seek to address pertain to game design issues that

have a detrimental effect on players’ well-being or that fail to satisfy their basic

psychological needs. Consequently, each Radiant Pattern should be accompanied

by a description of the game design issue that this pattern aims to address.

Context. Each pattern should be accompanied by a description of recommended

scenarios and game styles in which it can be applied. Given that patterns possess

distinct characteristics, it is essential to define their recommended use within

the game context to ensure the pattern’s effectiveness in achieving its intended

positive outcomes.

Proposed Solution. As a solution to a recurring problem, each description

should present how the RP can effectively address the identified problem. The

proposed solution outlines how game mechanics can be implemented to enable

the pursuit of development goals while ensuring foundational player well-being.

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 121

Avoiding Decrease in Autonomy, Relatedness and Competence. The

pattern then continues with a description of how it supports the player’s basic

psychological needs. The three fundamental needs—autonomy, competence, and

relatedness—are addressed individually, with a thorough exposition of how each

pattern positively impacts them. These descriptions elucidate the manner in

which the needs are supported independently, thereby ensuring that the fulfill-
ment of one need does not interfere with the fulfillment of others.

Watch For. If implemented improperly or outside of the intended context, the

efficacy of patterns may be compromised. Therefore, it is essential to include

a description of how to minimize predictable risks, avoid frustrating implemen-
tations, and highlight examples of poor applications of the pattern. Additional

warnings should also be provided to help designers recognize and prevent poten-
tial issues.

Example of Implementations: Failing and Matching the RP Criteria.

As an extension of the “watch for” section, it is important to present examples

of pattern implementations that align with the criteria defined for Radiant Pat-
terns. Likewise, it is necessary to provide examples where the implementation

does not meet these criteria. This enables a more in-depth discussion on imple-
mentation strategies and key considerations to help mitigate potential obstacles.

Good Examples. As the identified patterns are based on mechanics already

present in existing games, it is essential to present a comprehensive list of games

that effectively incorporate these patterns. A visual representation of the pat-
tern’s practical application within a game can enrich the definition and offer

game developers a better understanding of its practical implementation.

5.2 Radiant Pattern Example

In this subsection, we demonstrate the application of the proposed RP structure

and present a game mechanic found in existing games that meets the criteria for

a Radiant Pattern. This Radiant Pattern is called World Creation. Below, we

present its documentation as a Radiant Pattern following the structure (Table 2 ).

Name. World Creation - Allows players to create and customize scenarios and

stages.

Problem. Players may have too little agency, creative paths, or channels of

meaningful expression within the boundaries of a game’s pre-determined param-
eters. Inert game worlds can limit long-term play and social interaction based

on shared experiences.

Context. Digital games where players interact with game systems and poten-
tially each other. Applicable across various genres (sandbox, platformers, creative

suites).

Proposed Solution. Allows players to create, customize, and collaborate on or

share scenarios using readily accessible tools and resources, deliberately avoiding

Avoiding Decrease in Autonomy, Relatedness, and Competence

Autonomy - World Creation promotes autonomy by giving players plenty of

control and freedom (the autonomy to customize their own environments) over

their creations and their interaction with the game world. It prevents reducing

sual evidence and real-time insights. A shared template organized the materials
to ensure coherence while acknowledging researcher analytical perspective.
We analyzed the data through a reflexive thematic approach grounded in
the RP definition, identifying recurring patterns, ambiguities, and design ele-
ments satisfying Phase II invariants that aligned with or diverged from intended
need support. This phase generated illustrative cases and clarification notes that
informed further refinement and stabilization of the Radiant Pattern catalog.

4 Findings and Decurrent Improvements

This section presents results from the collaborative workshop, curated refinement
sessions, and exploratory autoethnography. Game titles appear in italics (e.g.,

Super Mario Maker ), and pattern names are underlined (e.g., Creative Suite).

4.1 Baseline Radiant Patterns Required Structural Refinement

Workshop results revealed that while original patterns had the necessary infor-
mation, the template organization obscured alignment with RP definitions. Par-
ticipants emphasized the need to revise titles for specificity, structure patterns
into levels for genre flexibility, and improve the template to clarify components.
Two participants (P01, P02) highlighted the need to revise the titles of the
initial set for quick and clear identification of what each pattern addressed, par-
ticularly for Free Pet Care, Different Difficulty, and World Creation to support
quicker identification. As one noted: ’[P02]: we were revising it to make it more
related to the idea of a companion rather than a pet, because "pet care" strongly
evokes the idea of taking care of it. ’
Descriptions also lacked explicit references to basic psychological needs, hin-
dering practical use. This concern is reflected in P01’s statement: ’[P01]: It is
important for the title to be more specific. It should be more distinctive and re-
fer to the names of the elements from Self-Determination Theory ’. These issues
required changes across the entire set to ensure consistency and standardization.
Although examples were generally clear, four of five participants argued that
structuring patterns into levels was necessary due to cross-genre complexity. P04
noted difficulty applying Different Difficulty to souls-like games
3
: “[P04]: Dark
Souls style games are meant to be difficult. So it’s not only about the developer’s
goal of profit or engagement, you also have to consider the narrative objectives
that the game itself proposes .” P02 similarly argued that World Creation was too
broad: “[P02] World Creation involves many things. For example, if I say ’allow
players to create scenarios using a set of tools’, that’s one thing. Customization
starting from something that already exists, is another....There are particularities
within these interactions that also address different elements .”
To accommodate these contexts, participants proposed a tiered structure
inspired by WCAG [55]: ’[P01]: Like in WCAG, where you have Level A, AA

3 
The term “Soulslike” describes games that resemble the Dark Souls series, typically
featuring clear goals combined with high difficulty and multiple obstacles.

10 Darin et al.

RP2 - Free Pet Care changes to Companion : The term pet was too narrow
to cover the variety of companions in games. Companion broadens the
scope to include animal, human, technological, or symbolic entities with
decorative, narrative, or functional roles.
RP3 - Item Evolution changes to Progression : The original name restricted
the pattern to items. It was reframed to emphasize perceived progress
and achievement, decoupling it from exclusive item-based mechanics.
RP4 - World Creation changes to Creative Suite : The initial title centered
on world-building and did not reflect the range of creative experiences
in games. Creative Suite broadly encompasses player-generated content
such as customization, level design, system creation, and worldbuilding.
RP5 - Color Hint changes to Visual Support : Hint risked being interpreted
as tutorial guidance rather than gameplay affordances. Visual Support
broadens the scope beyond color cues and better reflects its role in miti-
gating visually blocking elements.
RP6 - Different Difficulty changes to Adaptive Challenge : The original
name suggested only player-controlled difficulty adjustments. The revised
title captures both manual adjustments and adaptive responses to differ-
ent player profiles and play styles.
By introducing these rules and applying them to the baseline RP set, we
promote clearer pattern identification without restricting patterns to specific
contexts, enabling expansion across settings. This supports future contextual
variants while preventing ambiguity that could hinder practical application.

Defining Hierarchical Scaling and Contextual Variants for RPs Discus-
sion revealed that original RPs failed to account for genre-specific constraints,
platform limitations, or player profiles. Contextual differences, such as the transi-
tion from single-player to multiplayer, are not isolated exceptions but structural
adaptations required to maintain the pattern’s efficacy. By analyzing these re-
quirements, we established two pragmatic rules for framework expansion:
1. Progressive Requirement Scaling : Structure pattern application into
hierarchical tiers, each representing increasing psychological need satisfaction
from a baseline of non-frustration.
2. Environment-Based Subclassing : Define structural variants that adapt
universal levels to specific gameplay contexts (e.g., genre, mode, platform)
without changing core logic.
These rules allow a more precise integration across varied RP titles. For
instance, the core mechanic of Companion requires different implementations
for decorative mascots in The Sims compared to combat partners in World of
Warcraft . Similarly, Creative Suite spans a broad design space—from aesthetic
customization to complex scenario sharing—that cannot be addressed by a single
description without losing developer utility.

Beyond Dark Patterns in Games 11

Following progressive scaling, patterns are organized into universal applica-
tion levels. Level L1 establishes the ethical floor of non-frustration. While L1
represents standard practice, i.e., its inclusion in the framework identifies it as a
necessary boundary against deceptive monetization or retention tactics, L2 and
L3 progressively enhance need satisfaction. For example, Open Gate includes
L1 – Safety (automatic progress saving), L2 – Autonomy (intentional stopping),
and L3 – Competence (visual feedback reinforcing achievement).
The use of environment-based subclassing through variants ensures extensi-
bility. This dual structure allows practitioners to add contextual implementations
to the RP catalog while preserving each pattern’s conceptual identity.

An Updated Radiant Pattern Framework Workshop evaluations and re-
finement sessions confirmed that original pattern descriptions lacked the struc-
tural rigor required for industry application. The primary failure involved the
conflation of developer goals with player outcomes, which obscured how specific
design choices support ethical objectives. Furthermore, the absence of explicit
dimensions like genre or platform prevented the framework from capturing the
structural adaptations necessary for diverse play environments. Table 3 presents
the resulting template. This systematic structure reorganizes the Radiant Pat-
tern Framework, ensuring that every RP added to the catalog supports consistent
application and future extensibility without fragmenting conceptual integrity.
To ensure scalability of the RP framework, we defined four pragmatic rules
for the RP template:
1. Goal–Outcome Decoupling : Separate developers’ technical goals from

Player Problems (the experiential goals or need frustrations addressed).
2. Multi-Dimensional Scoping : Specify target actors and context to avoid
vague terminology and support diverse settings.
3. Invariant–Variant Duality : Define core properties (Invariants) that must
hold across adaptations to preserve identity, regardless of the Variant.
4. Traceable Need Satisfaction : Map each solution to hierarchical design
levels (L1–L3) to validate radiance through structural criteria.

4.3 Eliciting RPs from Play Experiences with Commercial Games

Autoethnographic results
4 
confirm that these patterns already appear within
successful commercial titles, though their presence does not yet validate the
framework as a production tool. Celeste [10] yielded eight instances: three for
Open Gate, four for Adaptive Challenge, and one for Companion. A researcher
diary entry noted: ’ the dialogues contribute a lot to building the relationship ’.
While the current iteration prioritizes levels for autonomy and competence, these
dialogue-driven instances confirm the relatedness dimension as a priority for fu-
ture lexicon expansion. While this iteration stabilizes autonomy and competence,

4 
Table of Identified Patterns available in our dataset

Beyond Dark Patterns in Games 15

aiming to address the semantic fragmentation in characterizing and identifying
these patterns.
The autoethnography identified RPs in released games, confirming their real-
world presence. This analysis serves as a discovery method, though validating the
framework’s use during active development remains a future requirement. Just
as DPs were identified through critical observation of manipulative practices in
the game industry[56], analyzing game structures through the RPs framework
allowed researchers to identify design practices that either avoid needs frustration
or support the fulfillment of basic psychological needs. The structural evolution
of the RP framework from generalized formulations to context-specific variants
addresses a core challenge in player experience research which is the inability to
account for unique, genre-specific interactions [28].
By establishing universal levels alongside these variants, the Radiant Pat-
terns framework a contextually-specific approach, recognizing that the ethical
impact of a mechanic is grounded in the unique characteristics of its gameplay
environment[3]. It is important to clarify that the Universal Levels (L1-L3) are
intended as a methodological baseline rather than a claim of universal experi-
ence. While the experiential reality of a patterns varies wildly between genres,
such as the difference between competence in a sandbox and a soulslike, the re-
quirement to not frustrate basic psychological needs remains the common ethical
denominator. Hence, the RP variants allow the lexicon to remain stable while
respecting these diverse contextual boundaries identified in the literature.
The common lexicon aims to offer a systematic alternative to rapid-response
research triggered by technology panics [41]. Yet, a shared vocabulary is a tool
for interaction design, not a solution for all ethical challenges. Systemic issues
such as game worker welfare, harassment, and online toxicity require regulatory
and cultural interventions that lie beyond the scope of interaction design [27].
Besides, identifying these new mechanics through autoethnography does not
automatically qualify them as Radiant Patterns. This is why they are referred
on findings as candidate RPs. Identifying an RP requires evidence of recurrence,
which establishes it as a pattern[2], as well as discussion and coherence with the
components defined by the framework. This distinction creates a logical need for
the Radiant Patterns Catalog (Section 5). Because a single autoethnographic
instance cannot confirm a pattern, and a 10-hour sample may not capture the
full systemic depth of complex titles, the Catalog serves as a filter where these
initial observations are flagged for further verification. The ’candidate’ ideas
are subjected to a verification protocol. This ensures that only those designs
proven to be recurring and ethically sound are finalized, transforming subjective
observations into community-validated design knowledge. Expert observation
may result in false positives, reinforcing the need for the Catalog’s collaborative
verification protocol in which the practical application of these patterns can be
observed, analyzed, and discussed collectively.
Current constraints include the absence of longitudinal testing. Establishing
the RP framework and catalog provides the technical foundation needed to move
toward support for positive impact. Yet, the RPs Catalog is the digital infrastruc-

try conflict. A next step in the evolution of Radiant Patterns would be to explore

how they can generate a return for the game industry, addressing the advantages

of Deceptive Patterns and making them more attractive to game developers.

This progress can be collaborative as Radiant patterns can be identified based

on players’ and researchers’ experiences with game mechanics. Applying the tem-
plate structure proposed in this work makes it possible to systematize the cre-
ation and documentation of these patterns. Thus, the Human-Computer Inter-
action (HCI) community and game developers can collaborate to identify and

refine new Radiant Patterns. This collaboration could lead to the development of

an open repository of standards, strengthening the creation of a gaming industry

guided by ethical principles and committed to promoting player well-being.

6.5 Study Limitations

Although a refined definition and a detailed structure for operationalization is

presented, no evaluations with players have yet been conducted to validate the

direct effects of Radiant Patterns on well-being. The difficulty in isolating the

effects of design patterns from other gameplay elements such as graphics, sound,

and narrative also compromises the accuracy of such assessments. Generalizing

these results may also be affected, as players’ perceptions of the patterns can

vary depending on their gaming experience, personal profiles, prior exposure to

games, and awareness of the consequences of digital design patterns.

Another important limitation concerns the practical adoption of these pat-
terns by the game industry. Although they offer an ethical alternative to decep-
tive patterns, Radiant Patterns have not yet demonstrated concrete commercial

viability. The adoption of such patterns may not offer game designers an imme-
diate return in terms of their key objectives, including engagement metrics and

financial performance.

7 Conclusion

This paper presents a refined definition of radiant patterns and a documentation

structure that serve as a template to help game developers as well researches to

identify and empirically validate radiant patterns for his operationalization. This

structure is exemplified through the implementation of a example of a refined

defined Radiant Pattern.

As a refined pattern built upon the Self-Determination Theory, we rein-
force that the basic psychological needs of players—autonomy, competence, and

relatedness—are not compromised by detrimental design decisions, preserving

current levels of need satisfaction as well avoiding adverse effects directly associ-
ated with psychological harm. In this work, the authors extend an invitation to

the Human-Computer Interaction community to contemplate the development

of ethical alternatives to deceptive patterns by employing our systematic tool to

collaboratively identify those alternatives.

5 A Catalog of Games Radiant Patterns

The Radiant Patterns Catalog 
6 
is a structured knowledge system designed to
bridge player well-being research and game development practice. It operational-
izes the multidimensional framework of Universal Levels and Contextual Vari-
ants derived from our refinement sessions. The platform is organized around
context-driven filters that allow practitioners and researchers to query patterns
according to developer goals and player needs, directly reflecting Phase I findings
on genre specificity and application context. The system distinguishes between
Finalized RPs – those validated through formal verification – and Candidate
RPs, which are undergoing co-creation. This separation enables transparency re-
garding pattern maturity while allowing users to choose between peer-validated
standards and experimental alternatives. Filters include variant-based con-
texts (e.g., Single-Player, Multiplayer) and development goals (e.g., preserving
progress, managing companions), all within the boundaries of the RP framework.
A core contribution of the platform is its tiered visualization of pattern levels,
translating abstract psychological principles into concrete design examples. Each
pattern presents its Universal Application Levels (L1, L2, L3) alongside a visual
carousel of real-world game instances. These examples, combined with textual
explanations, function as a semiotic bridge that illustrates how an RP manifests
across levels without requiring deep SDT expertise.
To ensure scalability, the platform includes a collaboration module en-
abling repository expansion. It supports two entry types: structured submissions ,
where contributors propose new patterns or variants using the RP template
vocabulary; and problem-based contributions , which document recurring design
problems requiring ethical alternatives. All submissions are flagged as Candi-
dates and remain visible but distinct from validated RPs until reviewed through
the governance process, preserving transparency while maintaining reliability.
To safeguard integrity, we propose a governance model in which community-
proposed RPs undergo a formal verification protocol modeled after the collabo-
rative workshops described in this paper. Sessions involving both academic and
industry specialists assess submissions against defined RP Invariants. Rather
than binary acceptance, proposals return to contributors for iterative refine-
ment, ensuring that candidate patterns remain accessible while being polished
into finalized standards. We invite volunteers from academia and industry to
participate as reviewers. Although reliance on a self-selected community may
introduce selection bias or uneven SDT expertise, the documentation template
serves as the primary objective check. By requiring mechanics to be mapped to
specific needs, it reduces the risk of subjective gatekeeping.

automatically qualify them as Radiant Patterns. This is why they are referred

components defined by the framework. This distinction creates a logical need for
the Radiant Patterns Catalog (Section 5). Because a single autoethnographic
instance cannot confirm a pattern, and a 10-hour sample may not capture the
full systemic depth of complex titles, the Catalog serves as a filter where these
initial observations are flagged for further verification. The ’candidate’ ideas
are subjected to a verification protocol. This ensures that only those designs
proven to be recurring and ethically sound are finalized, transforming subjective
observations into community-validated design knowledge. Expert observation
may result in false positives, reinforcing the need for the Catalog’s collaborative
verification protocol in which the practical application of these patterns can be
observed, analyzed, and discussed collectively.

the RP framework and catalog provides the technical foundation needed to move
toward support for positive impact. Yet, the RPs Catalog is the digital infrastruc-

ture that supports the collaborative verification process, converting community
observations into systematized, positive solutions. It offers the technical basis
for researchers and developers to co-create a repository of well-being-supportive
design patterns. This reinforces the development of a community centered on
ethical game design practices, fostering knowledge sharing and the adoption of
approaches focused on player well-being.

This work evolves the RP framework by shifting focus to the structural non-
frustration of basic psychological needs through a refined lexicon, tiered levels,
and standardized templates. These components establish a system to connect
ethical research with game development practice. While this version lacks longi-
tudinal data, relies on a small expert-centric sample, and excludes systemic issues
like worker welfare or online toxicity, it establishes the technical foundation for
future industry-led verification.

dimension based on observed dialogue-driven instances, and implementing the
collaborative verification protocol to transition candidate patterns into finalized

Avoiding Decrease in Autonomy, Relatedness and Competence. The

pattern then continues with a description of how it supports the player’s basic

psychological needs. The three fundamental needs—autonomy, competence, and

relatedness—are addressed individually, with a thorough exposition of how each

pattern positively impacts them. These descriptions elucidate the manner in

which the needs are supported independently, thereby ensuring that the fulfill-
ment of one need does not interfere with the fulfillment of others.

Watch For. If implemented improperly or outside of the intended context, the

efficacy of patterns may be compromised. Therefore, it is essential to include

a description of how to minimize predictable risks, avoid frustrating implemen-
tations, and highlight examples of poor applications of the pattern. Additional

warnings should also be provided to help designers recognize and prevent poten-
tial issues.

Example of Implementations: Failing and Matching the RP Criteria.

As an extension of the “watch for” section, it is important to present examples

of pattern implementations that align with the criteria defined for Radiant Pat-
terns. Likewise, it is necessary to provide examples where the implementation

does not meet these criteria. This enables a more in-depth discussion on imple-
mentation strategies and key considerations to help mitigate potential obstacles.

Good Examples. As the identified patterns are based on mechanics already

present in existing games, it is essential to present a comprehensive list of games

that effectively incorporate these patterns. A visual representation of the pat-
tern’s practical application within a game can enrich the definition and offer

game developers a better understanding of its practical implementation.

5.2 Radiant Pattern Example

In this subsection, we demonstrate the application of the proposed RP structure

and present a game mechanic found in existing games that meets the criteria for

a Radiant Pattern. This Radiant Pattern is called World Creation. Below, we

present its documentation as a Radiant Pattern following the structure (Table 2 ).

Name. World Creation - Allows players to create and customize scenarios and

stages.

Problem. Players may have too little agency, creative paths, or channels of

meaningful expression within the boundaries of a game’s pre-determined param-
eters. Inert game worlds can limit long-term play and social interaction based

on shared experiences.

Context. Digital games where players interact with game systems and poten-
tially each other. Applicable across various genres (sandbox, platformers, creative

suites).

Proposed Solution. Allows players to create, customize, and collaborate on or

share scenarios using readily accessible tools and resources, deliberately avoiding

124 L. S. Filho and T. Darin

and expression is untethered from unreasonable grinding or monetary expenses.

This strongly encourages autonomy and establishes a foundation for competency

development.

Intuitive Design and Clear Feedback. Offering user-friendly, responsive

tools with clear feedback and adequate tutorials (integrated into the gameplay

itself) gives players a sense of empowerment. This directly supports competence

by making the tools learnable and usable and minimizing frustration with the

interface.

Facilitating Sharing and Community. Emphasize being able to post and

discover/play community content easily. Making sharing and discovery easy and

satisfying enhances the entire creative ecosystem and avoids the frustrating trend

of isolating creators. This might include sharing full games and experiences.

Optional Unlocks By Engaging Play. While fundamental tools ought to be

readily available, providing optional cosmetic qualities, upgraded parts, or the-
matic elements as rewards for participation in many of the game’s aspects (which

do not solely revolve around grinding) might suit the RP model. This would pro-
vide room for progress objectives without restricting required creativity, perhaps

augmenting players’ senses of competence as they acquire fresh creative possi-
bilities.

Good Examples. The LittleBigPlanet game franchise has a “Create Mode”

that allows players to create levels using tools provided by the developers. These

levels can be accessed by other players if they are published to the community.

Similarly, the Super Mario Maker franchise allows players to create levels using

items and resources from other games in the Mario franchise (Fig. 1 ). Dreams

goes even further, allowing players to create entire games and experiences, both

visually and musically.

Fig. 1. Super Mario Maker as an example of World Creation Pattern.

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 127

developers recognize their potential harm [ 1 ], which illustrates a complex indus-
try conflict. A next step in the evolution of Radiant Patterns would be to explore

how they can generate a return for the game industry, addressing the advantages

of Deceptive Patterns and making them more attractive to game developers.

This progress can be collaborative as Radiant patterns can be identified based

on players’ and researchers’ experiences with game mechanics. Applying the tem-
plate structure proposed in this work makes it possible to systematize the cre-
ation and documentation of these patterns. Thus, the Human-Computer Inter-
action (HCI) community and game developers can collaborate to identify and

refine new Radiant Patterns. This collaboration could lead to the development of

an open repository of standards, strengthening the creation of a gaming industry

guided by ethical principles and committed to promoting player well-being.

6.5 Study Limitations

Although a refined definition and a detailed structure for operationalization is

presented, no evaluations with players have yet been conducted to validate the

direct effects of Radiant Patterns on well-being. The difficulty in isolating the

effects of design patterns from other gameplay elements such as graphics, sound,

and narrative also compromises the accuracy of such assessments. Generalizing

these results may also be affected, as players’ perceptions of the patterns can

vary depending on their gaming experience, personal profiles, prior exposure to

games, and awareness of the consequences of digital design patterns.

Another important limitation concerns the practical adoption of these pat-
terns by the game industry. Although they offer an ethical alternative to decep-
tive patterns, Radiant Patterns have not yet demonstrated concrete commercial

viability. The adoption of such patterns may not offer game designers an imme-
diate return in terms of their key objectives, including engagement metrics and

financial performance.

7 Conclusion

This paper presents a refined definition of radiant patterns and a documentation

structure that serve as a template to help game developers as well researches to

identify and empirically validate radiant patterns for his operationalization. This

structure is exemplified through the implementation of a example of a refined

defined Radiant Pattern.

As a refined pattern built upon the Self-Determination Theory, we rein-
force that the basic psychological needs of players—autonomy, competence, and

relatedness—are not compromised by detrimental design decisions, preserving

current levels of need satisfaction as well avoiding adverse effects directly associ-
ated with psychological harm. In this work, the authors extend an invitation to

the Human-Computer Interaction community to contemplate the development

of ethical alternatives to deceptive patterns by employing our systematic tool to

collaboratively identify those alternatives.

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 123

Watch For. A properly designed World Creation pattern would go out of its

way not to make fundamental creative tools conditional on excessive grinding or

direct payment. These are predicted risks for psychological harm (frustration,

exploitation) and are set patterns that necessarily thwart autonomy (loss of

liberty to create) and competence (progress feels hindered or artificial). The

bottom line for maintaining the World Creation framework as an RP is that

fundamental creative tools, basic elements, and the main ability to save and

share creations should not be expressly limited by financial constraints or only

provided through substituting payment for excessive grind. Monetization should

target optional enhancements, platform access, or adjacent community offerings,

all while keeping the basic act of creation separate and proficiency-dependent,

without creating financial pressure as a barrier to core activity.

Example of Implementations

Implementations Failing to Meet RP Criteria

To gate key components , required mechanisms, or the storage and sharing

of works behind boring, repetitive gameplay cycles (grind) or outright financial

expenditure. Imposing costs on essential tools would directly hinder autonomy,

as players are unable to realize their creative vision and competence freely, given

that the capacity to construct is unjustly restricted by external factors unrelated

to creative ability.

Poor implementations or Obfuscated Tools. The presentation of creation

tools that are poorly designed, buggy, lack basic features (like precise positioning

or undo functions), or are poorly documented undermine the player’s feeling of

competency, making them feel hampered in their ability to realize their ideas

because of limitations imposed by the tools instead of limitations imposed by

their skill level. Additionally, this reduces autonomy by rendering specific forms

of creative expression effectively impossible.

Restrictive Sharing and Discovery Mechanisms. When sharing works is

difficult, discovery of the works of others is inadequately supported (e.g., no

search/curation), or there are arbitrary restrictions on what or how much can

be shared, the relatedness dimension of the pattern is strongly negated. This can

be annoying, as many creators’ motivations include sharing and communicating

with the community. Restricting this diminishes the value of creation.

Insufficient Scaffolding of Sophisticated Tools. Very sophisticated creation

environments can overwhelm users if not backed up by solid tutorials, progres-
sive feature unlocking, or overt guidance (scaffolding). Unveiling tremendous

complexity without help can consistently lead to frustration and abandonment,

precluding competence.

Implementations In line with RP Criteria

Accessible Core Creative Suite. To make a robust set of core creation

elements and tools immediately available to the player. Though some extra

pieces may be gated behind an upfront barrier, the core capacity for creation

Operationalizing Radiant Patterns 125

6 Challenges, Perspectives and Limitations

As we refined the definition and template of Radiant Patterns, we encountered

challenges related to their perception, application, and evaluation. Key issues

included variations in player interpretation, measuring their impact on well-
being, and balancing industry goals with ethical design. We also highlighted the

importance of collaboration between academia and developers for their effective

adoption.

6.1 Players Perception on Radiant Patterns

Our perception of radiant pattern is grounded in the intention behind their

design: to counteract the harmful effects of deceptive patterns. We expect this

mitigation to occur because radiant patterns align with Self-Determination The-
ory, a fundamental theory for promoting player well-being. However, we acknowl-
edge that each player’s perception can affect their experience of these patterns.

First, as [ 41 ] highlighted, digital literacy regarding ethics in game develop-
ment directly affects understanding of these patterns. Player who are familiar

with the SDT are more likely to distinguish between positive and deceptive

patterns. Second, experienced players may already be familiar with deceptive

patterns from their gameplay history. As such, they recognize these patterns as

commonly used strategies to engage players, often without fully understanding

their consequences.

We cannot be overly confident that these patterns will work in every context

which they were designed. Since these patterns were developed empirically, fur-
ther evaluation is necessary to understand their actual effects, especially when

considering different player profiles. Players with certain profiles may react dif-
ferently to the present of such patterns. Some players may even prefer these

patterns, despite the potential negative consequences, while other players didn’t

even download the game if they know that these patterns are presented in the

game.

6.2 A Balance Between Deceptive and Radiant Patterns

We recognize that the terms “deceptive patterns” and “radiant patterns” may

reflect a dualistic perspective that associates radiance with virtue and darkness

with harm or unethical behavior. However, our goal is not to undermine the

industry by proposing these patterns, but rather to create a balance between

industry interests and player well-being – an ongoing challenge in developing

such design approaches.

Our refined definition comes from the understanding that, while the initial

conceptualization of Radiant Patterns positioned them partly as an antithesis to

Game Dark Patterns, we believe this perspective warrants refinement. Viewing

Radiant Patterns solely as the opposite of Dark Patterns might inadvertently

restrict their scope. In our novel proposed perspective, a design could avoid

dark patterns yet fail to be ‘radiant’ if it does not consciously engage with

We did not find any statistically significant difference in any app category. Di
Geronimo and Hidaka also failed the test and did not find any correlations
between the number of DPs and the app categories. This test supports the
hypothesis of the pervasive nature of DPs. A Kruskal-Wallis test ( χ
2
